p.t: In short
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Plan **five different offers** for Q4, one for each holiday promotion. Never repeat the same discount.
Set the **start and end dates** before you write any sale text or make any images.
Promise only **delivery dates you can really meet**. Check your supplier and shipping times first.

After each promotion, **put your normal offer back** on the site and undo the sale changes.
Keep a **default offer** live all the time, such as 5 or 10 percent off.
When a promotion ends, **switch back** to the default offer and undo every promotion change on the site.

Before a big sale, **raise the discount in steps**: 20%, 30%, 40%, 50%, 60%.
For Black Friday and Cyber Monday, **60-70%** works best. Above 80%, fewer visitors buy.
Offer arsenal and monthly rotation
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Build an offer arsenal: a list of at least four offers you can pull from whenever you need one.
The list is the pool you rotate through over the year.
Brainstorm ideas without pricing them first, then check each idea's cost and margin before scheduling it. Keep the list written down so you can reuse, adjust and pull from it each month.
A monthly offer-brainstorming exercise can produce around 12 unique offers, more than the five needed for Q4. Keep a running list so you always have spares.

Plan Q4 offers in this order:
1. Brainstorm about 12 possible promotions.
2. Select five and assign one to each holiday.
3. Record the offer, eligibility and theme for each promotion in an offer calendar planned a year in advance.
4. For each promotion, check the historical best-performing email subject lines and ad headlines, ranked by opens, clicks and sales, and pick those that fit the brand.

5. Use the same message in the email subject lines and in the remarketing ad headlines.
6. Set up the email segment and the remarketing audiences, then launch.
Promote one offer per month. Offers can be recycled and reused throughout the year.
Run only one offer per month. Proven offers can be recycled every quarter or every six months, ideally with a new twist, but not repeated every month.
** Rotate offers monthly rather than repeating the same promotion. Two promotions in the same month, such as during November, are not too much.
** Rotate the type of promotion each month, such as a bundle, a fixed percentage off, or something else, instead of repeating one offer.
Vary promotions across the year instead of repeating the same discount on each holiday.
Choose the deal, such as a free gift, a free item, or a buy-one-get-one-free offer tied to a supplier deal, based on what the target customer wants.
Offer arsenal and monthly rotation (continued)
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Monthly promotions usually run for three to five days, announced to the email list and on social media.

Each month can follow a fixed theme. Example rotating offer calendar, one offer per month and reused across the year:
**September**: 10% off

**October**: Free white glove delivery
**November**: Bonus gift with all orders over $1,000
**December**: Free bonus gift with all orders
Offer calendar layout: one row per month, with a scheduled promotion window of 3 to 5 days. Recycled offers can be reused in later quarters with a new twist.

**Free bonus item (e.g. a recipe pack)**
Offer eligibility: Any purchase of a specific starter kit
Scheduled month: June

Notes: Tie the note to an upcoming holiday, e.g. a July 4th barbecue
**Free physical product (e.g. a book)**

Offer eligibility: Any qualifying order
Scheduled month: July
Notes: Short personal note explaining the gift

**Prize entry (e.g. a trip)**
Offer eligibility: Any order above $300 enters the customer in the draw
Scheduled month: August
Notes: Note explaining the entry and the prize
Four promotion types exist: monetary promotions, bundles, physical product bonuses and digital product bonuses. Each is used to turn existing leads who have not bought into customers.
A sale or promotion section can be linked in the header and refreshed about once a month. Sales are allowed when a supplier is discontinuing a product or when a promotion bundles extra items.
Sales mainly during Black Friday, with otherwise selling out each collection before moving to the next. Do not discount constantly.
Sources differ on how many sales a year to run. Monthly promotions are advised in the rotation rules above. Sell-out-by-collection with Black Friday as the main sale is advised in.
Use the monthly rhythm for a rotating offer arsenal, and the collection rhythm for a range sold in collections.
Offer types and gift structures
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Percent-off offers are the simplest monthly promotion.
Raise your usual coupon for a short window, for example from 5 percent to 10 percent off all orders.
Fixed-amount offers work best on higher-priced products, for example save 50 dollars on all orders over 500 dollars.
Free expedited shipping works well in November and December, when customers worry about delivery before the holidays.
Promote a cutoff time, for example 5 p.m. for same-day or 24-hour dispatch, or a supplier ship-by date about a week before Christmas.
It can be run for only part of the catalog if the supplier does not offer it store-wide.
Buy-one-get-one-free offers work especially well in November around Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Shoppers buy extra units as gifts, or buy two and keep one and give one away.
A bundle promotion can run for roughly one week within a chosen month, not the whole month. Example: a golf bag sold at $400 with a $100 carrier upgrade.
A single $500 bundle that adds golf balls, a glove and a cleaning kit is a plausible one-week offer.
A bundle can include a free gift and a free ebook download, shown clearly in the ad so the customer sees the deal immediately.
Choice offer: the customer picks one of two free gifts. It keeps a product offer fresh and can rescue results when the old offer is worn out.
Examples: "Pick your free gift: a travel pouch or a bottle of cleaner with any order." and "Choose one free bonus: an extra case or a matching cable with your purchase."
Seasonal relabelling: keep the same discount and shipping offer, but rename it for the season, such as Black Friday or Cyber Monday, to make it look new.
Examples: 10% off plus free shipping for Black Friday; 10% off plus free shipping for Cyber Monday week. Older advice (2018).
Tie promotions to current events, holidays or seasonal moments where possible.
The more timely and relevant the promotion, the more interest and urgency it creates and the more likely older leads will convert.
Any seasonal reason can justify a discount event, including Halloween, a spring sale or a holiday. Short, recurring sales give buyers a reason to act now.
Keep the offer clear and time-limited so the reason to buy stays believable.
Offer types and gift structures (continued)
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Non-discount promotions can compete with large retailers, for example free white glove shipping, free expedited delivery for holiday timing, a raffle entry, or a bonus gift valued at around 100 dollars.
Older advice (2022).

Gift-with-purchase offers work during the holidays because the buyer can keep the gift or give it to someone else. The perceived value of the gift is often higher than its cost to the store. Older advice (2019).

**Gift-with-purchase formula for expensive products 
Pattern: a percentage discount combined with a free gift above a spend threshold.

Formula: Save [X]% and get a free [gift] on orders over $[threshold].
Example 1: Save 10% and get a free gift box on orders over $500.
Example 2: Save 15% and get a free set of RGB lights on orders over $1,500.
It works because the discount keeps the price appealing, the gift adds value the buyer can also give to someone else, and the threshold raises the average order.
Case: a store with high-margin products ran a holiday promotion giving a discount plus a free gift. The gifts included an $80 item and a set of RGB lights costing the store about $50.

The RGB lights offer was designed to push orders toward roughly $2,000 per customer.
**Free gift threshold
Pattern: a percentage discount plus a free gift on orders above a set amount, used only in peak sales periods by stores that already know their numbers.
The gift should be worth about $50 to $100 and be something the buyer can keep or give away.

Example 1: 10% off plus a free $80 gadget on orders over $1,000.
Example 2: 15% off plus a free $60 accessory on orders over $500.
Use it only where the store knows its average order value and margin, and only around holidays and sale days, not all year. Set the threshold above the average order value so the gift is affordable.
Gift-friendly offers can sell products that would not normally be bought as gifts.
During holiday shopping, buyers are already choosing presents for family, so a free gift removes one decision and pushes them toward your store.
Current figures (2024): A low-cost gift unrelated to the product, sent to buyers before the holiday deadline, can drive sales when inventory is limited.
The gift must be worth more to the customer than its cost of about $80 shipped.
Recycling offers
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Recycle proven offers two to three times a year, or every quarter or six months, rather than always creating new ones.
Repeat the offers that keep converting with the audience.
Sources differ on frequency. says two to three times a year; says every quarter or every six months, with a new twist; says cycle offer types at most about once a year,
and a BOGO that performed strongly at launch can fail on a repeat run. Use the once-a-year limit for offer types that have already faded.
Over 90% of visitors to a dropship store are first-time visitors who came from a paid ad for a specific product.
Because the audience is new each time, the same offer can be recycled very frequently without losing effect. Older advice (2018).

An offer that was used before can still work if it is packaged as a Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal.
Vary offer types and cycle them at most about once a year.
Repeated offers stop converting after a few weeks. Use a different offer for each promotion instead of the same discount, such as 5% off.
Repeating a 5 percent offer five times gets fewer responses because customers have already seen it.
Repeating the same discount on each promotion trains the audience to ignore it. Plan the offers in advance so none is recycled within the same quarter.
A holiday promotion using a repeated discount with a holiday name, such as 10 percent off with a holiday name, loses impact after the first use.
Each promotion in the quarter needs its own unique offer. Thanksgiving has no separate offer when it runs together with Black Friday.
Keep the offer you already run, such as free shipping, 5% off or 10% off, but change the coupon code to a holiday-related word.
Announce the holiday promotion on Facebook and send the same promotion to your email list. Holidays are a sales opportunity and not a reason to pause making money. Older advice (2019).
Audiences for promotions
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: A promotion works best when it is shown to a warm audience that has engaged for months, because the goodwill makes the offer feel natural.
A buy-one-get-one or free-add-on promotion timed to a holiday converts far better in front of that group than cold.
Examples in the same pattern: "Order a set of two candles this week and get a third free for the holidays" and "Buy the starter brewing kit now and get the seasonal ingredient pack free."
Time product offers to promotions and seasonal peaks such as summer, Black Friday and Christmas. Keep building the audience between them.
Regular content can mention products with a link in the description without being a sales video.

Wait before making offers to a new audience so it can grow and trust the brand. The example suggested about six weeks. Making offers right away is possible if resources exist to sell and grow at the same time.
Promotions to move less popular products or seasonal items work best when sent to warm audiences such as your email list and remarketing audiences of past visitors.
New visitors from cold traffic usually buy what they searched for, regardless of promotion. Older advice (2021).
Example warm audience size: around 2,000 people on your email list and around 10,000 people in a remarketing audience. Push promotions to those groups first rather than to new visitors.
Older advice (2021).
Run a discount or flash sale every month, targeted at one segment of the email list.
Revenue was higher in every month with a significant discount, so brands that fear discounting for premium image should test it.
Online competition for attention and inbox space makes a sale a strong tool.
Sales event opt-ins can stop visitors from buying immediately, because they wait for the event. Run them close to the event rather than too far in advance to limit that effect. Older advice.
Run giveaways before Black Friday. This builds early interest at low CPM, and the engaged audience can then be converted during Black Friday.
Source conflict on channel priority: for Black Friday and Cyber Monday in the first month of a new store with a small email list, storefront promotions matter more than email campaigns.
Audiences for promotions (continued)
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Make the store's promotions match the holiday, and add them once the first suppliers are live. Warm-audience targeting in applies to older stock and promotions aimed at existing buyers.
Promotions aimed at the store's existing buyers did not move slower products in one 2021 case.
Results were mediocre, and select brands on sale up to 20 percent off sold few units, while regular best sellers sold more. Older advice (2021).

Case, 2021: a store ran a tiered Black Friday promotion spending 400 dollars for 15 percent off, 800 dollars for 20 percent off and 1,200 dollars for 25 percent off, with average order value around 350 dollars.
The next month without promotions still produced more sales than December. Older advice (2021).
Store promotions perform differently from one another and affect monthly revenue, so plan a promotion calendar
and track results per promotion. Use the best-performing promotions as a baseline for future months.
Coupon codes on the store were valid on Wednesdays and Sundays, chosen because traffic is similar each day. The host did not split-test the days.
Use coupon codes tied to the holiday season, such as Black Friday, Cyber Monday or Xmas. Promote them in email, on social media pinned posts and in cover images. Older advice (2020).
Each offer promotion should run 3 to 5 days.
Use the shorter end when quantity is limited, and the longer end when you need more hype or when the purchase is a large decision for the audience.
Each promotion runs for 3 to 5 days, and the rest of the month the normal percentage discount applies. Example: a promotion may run from January 1 to January 5 only.
Use shorter promotions when quantity is limited. Example: when a supplier allows only 20 units, the offer runs for three days or until the 20 units sell out, whichever comes first.
Use a five-day promotion for big purchase decisions, high-ticket items or when more hype needs to be built.
For larger purchases, send one pre-promotion email before the offer starts to tell the audience something big is coming and prepare them for it.
Monthly promotions of 3 to 5 days can be run, tied to a holiday or event relevant to the niche. Promotions are typically used with promo codes rather than price changes.
Promotion duration and timing rules (continued)
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: A promotion with a real deadline, such as a holiday, creates urgency.
It can run for a single day or through a weekend, and it should be promoted with a sale announcement on the website and social media.
A 3-day Halloween promotion example: October 29 to October 31, 2024, with 10% off the whole store using the coupon code "happyhalloween",
and one promotional email each day of the sale window.

A holiday promotion can be run as a short fixed window, such as Monday to Friday of one week, with a percentage-off discount code for all customers. Set the start and end dates before writing any promotional copy.
Source conflict on length: a 3-to-5-day window is standard; a five-day window is for big-ticket items; a week-long window is used for Black Friday; a one-day window is used for Cyber Monday;
a 48-hour window is used for flash sales. Each applies to its own case.
Weekday rule: end offers on a weekday, and use Friday for the more expensive offers. Tie the promotion to current events or holidays where you can.
Plan promotions at least three months ahead, covering Halloween, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year, with one specific offer per event. Older advice (2022).
Holiday promotion routine, from 2019, applies when you have no unique offer ready: rename the existing discount code, and keep the same offer under a holiday code. Older advice (2019).
A holiday promotion can still be worthwhile when planned only about one week ahead.
In that case, a simple change such as renaming the existing discount code to a holiday word is enough, while a unique offer requires more lead time.
A holiday promotion can be assembled, configured, announced to your email list and posted to social media in approximately one hour.
A discount of 5% or 10% paired with a holiday-specific code (for example "MemorialDay" instead of a generic discount) has measurable impact even with a small audience; converting one
or two additional sales justifies the effort.
Holiday planning for the US calendar
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: U.S. holidays such as Memorial Day and the 4th of July, and monthly occasions,
provide recurring promotional triggers throughout the year.
A national holiday such as the 4th of July is a reason to run a special promotion that differs from everyday discounts. This applies only to stores that sell to customers in the US.
If there is no time for a unique holiday offer, the fastest starting point is renaming the existing discount code to a holiday word such as "July 4th", "freedom" or "fireworks".
Set that code to expire at the end of the promotion window.
A holiday promotion in the lesson ran for five days, from Monday 1 July to Friday 5 July, with the code expiring at midnight on the final day.

Normal promotion codes in the same business typically ended on Wednesday or Sunday.
4th of July promotion plan:
1. Create a holiday-themed promotion, or rename the existing discount code to a holiday word such as "July 4th", "freedom" or "fireworks".

2. Set the code to expire at the end of the five-day window, Friday 5 July in the example.
3. Show the code on the store and promote it to new visitors coming from ads.
4. Send promotion emails to the existing email list on every day of the window, from Monday to Friday.
5. Run static holiday remarketing ads to older website visitor audiences.
6. Run dynamic product ads to recent visitors who have not bought, excluding recent customers.
Start holiday promotions weeks early, since suppliers get busy, some close, and shipping carriers are backed up in the peak shipping period before Christmas.
Holiday offers should state the gift benefit clearly, such as a Christmas gift or a holiday promotion. Older advice (2019).
Holiday promotions were run on all dropshipping stores, so promotional calendars should be planned per store. Older advice (2019).
Holiday-specific bundles can be promoted earlier than the holiday, for example during Black Friday or Cyber Monday, since many people shop for gifts early.
Holiday bundles or special products do not need to wait until the holiday itself to be promoted.
Testing them earlier, for example during Black Friday or Cyber Monday, is worth doing because many people shop for Christmas during those events.
Q4 planning (Q4 = October to December, the last three months of the year)
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Prepare **five** unique offers for the Q4 promotion season.

A promotion is a sale or special deal for a set time.
Thanksgiving is a US holiday in late November. It falls inside the Black Friday promotion.
The five offers cover these events: Halloween, Black Friday with Thanksgiving, Cyber Monday, Christmas and New Year.
Run **five** unique offers across five promotions in Q4. Do not repeat the same discount.
Use five unique offers for the five holiday promotions. Do not repeat the same discount, such as **5% off**.
Repeated offers stop converting after a few weeks. Converting means turning visitors into buyers.
Each offer should give customers a different reason to buy **now**.
Plan a **promotion for each** Q4 event: Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Christmas and New Year.
Create the promotional images and promotional email copy (the written words) for each event **before it starts**.
If a store has no Black Friday promotion ready, it is getting late. It is still possible to plan and launch one **before the event**.
An existing store offer can be the basis for one of the five holiday promotions.
Examples: a site-wide discount code (one code for the whole store) or free premium white-glove shipping (premium delivery with careful handling).

Each promotion still needs a **different offer**, not the same discount repeated.
Plan at least the **next three months** covering the holidays.
To prepare holiday promotions:

1. List **every** holiday that can carry a promotion.
2. Choose **one offer** for each event.
3. Create the **Klaviyo emails** for each promotion. Klaviyo is an email tool for sending messages to customers.
Q4 planning (Q4 = October to December, the last three months of the year) (continued)
4. Create the images for **Facebook remarketing ads**. Remarketing ads are ads shown again to people who already visited your store.
5. Create the images for **Google display ads**. Google display ads are picture ads shown on websites in Google's network. Older advice (2022).
Set the **start and end dates** of the promotion before writing any promotional copy.
Use a **single discount code** for all customers, such as 10% off. A discount code is a code the customer types at checkout to get a discount.
Combine the discount code with a delivery promise before a holiday deadline.
Only promise a **delivery date you can actually meet**, based on your supplier (the company that sends you the products) and shipping times.
Q4 is estimated to add about **30 percent** to monthly revenue. Revenue is the total money from sales.

The actual gain **scales** with your current revenue level. Scaling means it rises in step with it.
Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales rise even **without** specific promotions.
Once the first suppliers are live (ready to sell), add holiday-relevant promotions on the store to boost sales further.
Change the sale reason every **three to four days**, following a calendar.
The sale reasons, in order: early November sale, 11.11, pre-Black Friday, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Christmas and end-of-year sale.

A monthly offer-brainstorming exercise (a session to think up deals) can produce around **12 unique offers**.
Keep a running list of ideas so you always have spares.

Black Friday and thanksgiving
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales start **before Black Friday** and end at **midnight on Cyber Monday**. Older advice (2021).
Long promotions tend to perform well. One planned campaign included **seven emails**. Older advice (2021).
Start Black Friday promotions and ads at least **one day before** Black Friday. Older advice (2022).
Start the Black Friday sale on the **Monday before Thanksgiving**. Run it through Black Friday. Do not extend it after the event.
Longer sale windows produced more sales in this approach.
Black Friday promotions perform better the longer they run. Start the sale before Thanksgiving, not after Black Friday.
A five-day email run from the Monday before Thanksgiving through Black Friday covers the Thanksgiving shopping window.
A Black Friday promotion can run as a **week-long event** that includes Thanksgiving Day as one of its days.
Combine Thanksgiving and Black Friday into one roughly **week-long** promotion. Do not run a month-long Black Friday event.
Start it on the Monday before Thanksgiving and end it on Black Friday.
Thanksgiving is a US-specific holiday. It is folded into the Black Friday promotion instead of getting its own campaign.
The Thanksgiving-day email is themed around the holiday and **repeats the discount code**.

For Black Friday and Cyber Monday, use **aggressive discounts** (deep, strong price cuts).
Discounts of **60 to 70 percent** perform best.
Discounts above **80 percent** tend to be seen as too good to be true and convert worse.
You may need to raise the product price beforehand. This keeps a margin you can afford. Margin is the money you keep after paying costs.
Escalating discount ladder (discounts that rise step by step) for an event: start one month before the event with **20% off**.
Then increase weekly to 30%, 40%, 50% and 60%.
Black Friday and thanksgiving (continued)
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Raise prices incrementally (in small steps) as discounts increase. This keeps your margin and justifies the perceived value of the offer.
Run your main event (Black Friday or Christmas) with **increasing offer pressure**.
Black Friday pricing on Google Shopping (Google's product listing area) depends on your **supplier agreements** (the contracts you have with suppliers). Older advice (2022).

Without a MAP restriction (MAP means minimum advertised price, the lowest price a brand lets you show), **lower the price in Shopify** (your store software). The lower price then shows in Google Shopping.

Older advice (2022).
A bundle offer (several products sold together) can run across the Black Friday to Cyber Monday window on the store. Older advice (2020).
Google Shopping ads stay **unchanged** during the bundle offer. Older advice (2020).
Promote the bundle on-site, through email and through remarketing. Do not promote it as a Shopping promotion. Older advice (2020).

Pre-sale momentum: build it with a **smaller offer** that grows toward Black Friday. Do not run a long sale that lasts for weeks.
Keep the **largest offer for Black Friday** itself.
A **24-hour sale extension** is a common Black Friday tactic. It is used especially by brands that rely on finding new customers.
A 24-hour sale extension **weakens urgency** (the feeling you must act now) if the messaging is careless.
Black Friday and Cyber Monday are a sales **dip-and-peak cycle** (sales drop, then rise).
A sales dip before Black Friday, and again in January and February, is a normal ebb and flow (ups and downs) for e-commerce (online selling).
Plan cash flow (money coming in and going out) around these dips. Do not react with panic.
Free express shipping is used near **shipping cut-off dates** (the last day to order and still arrive on time), for example before Black Friday.
Free express shipping lets customers receive orders earlier. It can squeeze a few extra days of sales.
Source note on Black Friday timing: the minimum for ads is **one day before** (2022). The planned start is the **Monday before Thanksgiving**. Both apply, with the Monday start as the plan.
Cyber Monday
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Cyber Monday works as a separate promotion, just **two days after Black Friday**.
Shoppers actively look for deals on Cyber Monday. They respond to repackaged offers (the same deal presented in a new way).
The 2024 calendar places Cyber Monday on **Monday 2 December**.
The 2025 calendar runs Cyber Monday on **Monday 1 December** as a one-day promotion.
The 2025 Cyber Monday promotion has **2 emails**, one in the morning and one in the evening. Remarketing runs all day.
Cyber Monday 2024: **early morning 2 December** and **about 17:00 on 2 December**, two emails, one day only.
Christmas promotions run **before Christmas**, not on Christmas Day.
The message says the buy-by date (the last day to order for delivery before the holiday) is closing.
Allow about **two weeks** for delivery. The emails go out in early to mid December.
The target is gift buyers. It is also customers who want high-ticket items (expensive products) or bulky items (large, heavy products), such as furniture or appliances, in time for the holiday.

The Christmas offer message is "order now to get your product before Christmas".
This message drives a **large spike** (a sudden rise in sales).

The message only works if suppliers can deliver within about **two weeks**.
Confirm **delivery times** first.
The Christmas promotion runs early in December. Shoppers have usually finished their spending by Christmas and are less active online then.
The main message is: order now to receive the product before Christmas. It drives a **sharp spike** in sales.
Example Christmas offer: discount code "xmas" gives **10 percent off**.
The same example pairs the code with a guarantee that the product will be delivered before Christmas.
This example only works if the supplier can deliver within about **two weeks**.
Christmas planning (continued)
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: The 2025 September call paired a **10% off code** with a guarantee that orders arrive before Christmas Day.
The 2024 Christmas calendar uses emails on **Monday 9, Wednesday 11 and Friday 13 December**.

The 2024 Christmas message is the last order date before Christmas.
The 2025 Christmas calendar runs from **Monday 8 December to Friday 12 December**.
The 2025 Christmas calendar uses **3 emails** on 8, 10 and 12 December.
Plan a Christmas sale for the **second week of December** so products can be delivered before the holiday. Older advice (2021).
Christmas offers can be **smaller than Black Friday**, because most of the buying is already done.
For a gift product, frame Christmas offers as **gifting**, not as a buy-one-get-one deal.
Use an **experiential gift** angle (a gift of an experience, not a thing) for buyers purchasing for a partner or themselves.
Example Christmas structure: **free express shipping** above a spend threshold (a minimum order amount).
The same example adds **around 20% off** site-wide, with an added gift to keep the momentum.
This should be **lower than the Black Friday deal**, so Black Friday buyers are not upset.
Gift wrapping: in Q4, offer **free gift wrapping** on high-tier bundles (the top, higher-level bundles) for giftable products.
Gift wrapping helps appeal to customers buying gifts for others.
Christmas packaging upsell (an extra paid add-on at checkout): offer a simple checkbox on the checkout cart for "Add holiday gift packaging".

The packaging costs **$0.50** to produce and sells for **$3-4**.
That adds **$3-4 profit per order** with no friction, if presented as a non-intrusive option.
Gift-friendly holiday bundle example: the main product plus a **free gift** and a **free ebook** download. An ebook is a digital book sent to the buyer.
Source note on gift wrap and packaging: free gift wrapping on high-tier bundles and a paid packaging checkbox at $3-4 are both valid. The first is a bundle benefit. The second is an add-on.
Holiday shipping cut-offs
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Stop selling Christmas-delivery products by **December 10-12** to guarantee shipping arrives before the holiday.
Cutoff dates prevent logistics bottlenecks (points where shipping slows down) in late December.

In late December, carrier capacity (how many packages delivery companies can handle) runs out.
Packages routinely arrive **after December 25**.
Non-seasonal products (jewelry, gadgets, apparel, lifestyle items) can keep selling past December 10-12 for Christmas gifts.

For those products, clearly state on the order page that **Christmas delivery is not guaranteed**.
Manage customer expectations through **follow-up emails**.
Seasonal products (Christmas ornaments, holiday decorations) must stop by **December 12**.
Stopping by December 12 prevents chargebacks (customers reversing a payment through their bank).
Organic channels (free traffic from search and social media, not paid ads) with higher margins tolerate late-delivery complaints better.

Paid ads with lower margins tolerate late-delivery complaints worse than organic channels.
Procedure for the cutoff:
1. Add a clear cutoff date to your website and order confirmation page (the page shown after a purchase), stating "Orders placed after [date] cannot be guaranteed Christmas delivery."
2. Include a **24-hour cancellation window** (time to cancel) on the confirmation email for customers who miss the cutoff.
3. Update your refund policy (your written rules for giving money back) to say that late-placed orders are **not eligible for refunds** due to shipping timing beyond your control.
Holiday deadline: in the 2025 calendar, Christmas runs **8 to 12 December**. This is within the 10-12 December cutoff range.
Expedited shipping (faster, paid delivery) offers: promote a cutoff time or a supplier ship-by date (the day the supplier must send the order) about **a week before Christmas**.
New Year
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Plan a New Year sale running from **December 31 into January 1** as an end-of-year promotion. Older advice (2021).
Avoid ending a promotion on **New Year's Day**, when buyers are usually least active.
Promotions should end on a **Friday**, because people are typically paid on Friday and spend more then.

Avoid ending on New Year's Day, when many shoppers are not buying.
The 2024 calendar runs New Year from **Monday 30 December**.

The 2024 calendar uses emails on Wednesday 1 January and Friday 3 January.
The 2024 calendar closes on **Friday 3 January**.
The 2025 calendar runs New Year from **31 December**, ending on **Friday 2 January 2026**. This is inferred (worked out, not stated). See calendar version A.

The 2025 calendar version B runs New Year from 31 December to **Friday 2 January**.
Source conflict: the 2021 advice ends the New Year sale on **January 1**.

The 2025 rule avoids ending on New Year's Day.
The later rule applies for new plans.
Close promotions on a **Friday** whenever possible. People are paid on Fridays and will otherwise ask for more time.
p.h: Closing the Friday rule for promotions

p.t: If a promotion must end on Wednesday or Thursday, send an **extra email on the Friday after** with the same offer extended by one day.
Promotions should end on a Friday because people are typically paid on Friday and spend more then.
Flash sales
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Flash sales are **time-limited promotions** (short sales with a fixed end time).
A flash sale uses a strong offer, such as a high-ticket item at a deep discount, a product bundle, or a trending seasonal product.

Pairing the time limit with **limited stock** creates urgency and triggers fear of missing out (FOMO).
Flash sale pattern: a promotion limited to a **fixed time window**.
The offer is built around a high-value item, such as a high-ticket item at a deep discount, a product bundle, or a trending seasonal product.

Pairing the time limit with limited stock creates urgency and taps into FOMO.
Example: a **48-hour sale** on a premium bundle with only **50 units** available.

Pair flash sales with a fixed window: a **48-hour window** on a premium bundle with 50 units.
Or use a **three-day window** when quantity is limited.
A monthly flash sale aimed at one email segment (a group of customers chosen to get one email) raises revenue in each month with a significant discount.
End-of-season discounts **clear stock** (products you must sell) that needs to leave quickly.
Shoppers also tend to wait for a sale before buying big-ticket items (expensive products) to get the largest savings.
End-of-season discounts clear out stock that needs to leave quickly.
Shoppers also delay purchases of big-ticket items until a sale. A seasonal discount captures that demand.

Mystery box: a "trust us" bundle used to clear unsold or weaker stock.
A mystery box only works if the brand keeps **enough real quality** in the box.

Otherwise the offer produces many returns and complaints.
Because it can usually be run **only once**, the box can be a limited edition created for that one promotion.
A brand that runs frequent sales can keep its image by building a strong brand experience around promotions.
This includes the ordering experience and merchandising (how products are arranged and shown). Plan it in advance so that discounting is part of the brand.

Clearance pricing for an extension: **70% off**.
The message for this clearance is "Almost out of stock: Black Friday stock still available".

Sell out each collection (a group of related products), then move on to the next one.
Do not discount constantly.
Extending a promotion
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Continue the promotion for **two weeks** after the event concludes.
In the extension period, use the message "Almost out of stock: Black Friday stock still available".

In the extension period, offer **70% off** to clear inventory (the products you hold).
A **24-hour sale extension** is a common Black Friday tactic.

A 24-hour sale extension **weakens urgency** if the messaging is careless.
Extend only the **same offer under the same terms**.

Adding deeper discounts, or a new offer for late buyers beyond early loyal customers, creates trouble.
Only change or extend an offer if the team can **execute it fully**.
A new offer means a website redo, updated email flows (automatic email series) and new ad creatives (new ad designs).

Extending a sale without proper execution hurts more than it helps.
A long sale period risks **offer fatigue** (customers get tired of the same deals).
If you extend the sale or change the offer after Black Friday, make it **exclusive to BFCM** (Black Friday and Cyber Monday).
This keeps the Black Friday offer's value.
Extension email: if an event ends on Thursday or Wednesday, send a **Friday email** with the same offer extended by one day.
The 2024 Halloween calendar uses a **Friday extension email on 1 November**, which is also the close.

Source conflict: the extension of the 2024 Halloween and Black Friday sales is **one day** under the Friday rule.
The two-week extension at 70% off is a clearance tactic.

Use the **one-day extension** for offers still in their promotion.
Use the **two-week clearance** only for stock to be cleared.
Closing a promotion
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t:
Close an expired offer (one whose dates have passed):
1. **Swap** the expired offer for your default offer (your normal everyday deal).

2. **Revert** (undo) every change made for the offer. Remove it from the notification bar (a thin message bar at the top of the site) and from the exit intent overlay (a pop-up shown when a visitor is leaving).
Revert the offer-dependent changes: custom product pages (special pages made for the offer), content pages (pages of text and information), edited product pages,
and the Bold Sales Motivator threshold display (the sales-goal display from that app).
Leaving an expired offer on the site sends shoppers to a **dead promotion**.
This includes banners, overlays, pages and progress trackers (bars or counters showing how much is left).

Always **swap in the default offer** and undo every promotion change.
Set the code to **expire at the end of the promotion window** (the time period when it works).

This keeps the code time-bound and relevant to the holiday.
Always keep a **default offer**, such as 5 or 10 percent off, live after a promotion ends.
People click promotional emails weeks later. They should still find something to buy at a fair price.

Promotions should end on **weekdays**, with **Friday** used for the more expensive offers.
Use a **sell-out close** (ending the offer when stock runs out) for limited stock.
The offer runs for **three days or until the 20 units sell out**, whichever comes first.
Keep a **default offer** live after every promotion ends. A default offer is a standing discount that is always on, such as 5 or 10 percent off.
When an offer ends, **switch** to the default offer and undo every promotion change on the site.
Discount depth
p.s: Promotion calendar, seasonal sales and Q4

p.t: Before a large event, **raise the discount in steps**: 20%, then 30%, 40%, 50%, 60%.
For Black Friday and Cyber Monday (the big US online sale days after Thanksgiving), **60-70%** performs best. Above 80%, the offer converts worse (fewer visitors buy).
For monthly promotions, **raise the usual coupon** for a short window, for example 5% to 10% off all orders. A coupon is a discount code the customer types in at checkout.
A repeated **5 percent** offer loses effect after several uses. Customers react less each time.
Source conflict (two sources give different numbers): 60-70% is the best range for Black Friday and Cyber Monday; the 70% clearance (a sale to sell old stock cheaply) is for stock after the event;
the monthly rule is a 5-10% coupon. Each figure applies to its own promotion type.
Run holiday promotions each month. Build ad campaigns (paid ads that run for a set period) for the biggest dates:
1. Plan a **promotion for each month**, with the largest ones around the holiday season.
2. Build ad campaigns for the specific promotion, such as Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Christmas or New Year.
3. Create the promotion in Google Shopping promotions (sales set up inside Google's shopping ads) where available.
Running a bundle promotion (several products sold together as one package) that is not a Google Shopping promotion:
1. Leave the Google Shopping ads **unchanged** for the promotion period.
2. Show a notification bar (a thin banner across the top of the website) that promotes the bundle during the promotion window (the set time the sale runs).
3. Use an exit intent overlay (a pop-up that appears when a visitor is about to leave) that announces the bundle price and links to the bundle page.
4. **Email** the store's list (your saved list of customer email addresses) about the bundle.
5. Run remarketing ads (ads shown again to people who already visited your site) on Facebook and Google to visitors who have not yet purchased.
